sections.title: The product problem
body: CashKaro had an established distribution audience, while a lending application still had to satisfy different lenders’ eligibility, KYC and servicing requirements. A customer could complete a form and still be sent towards an unsuitable lender. The product problem included the handoff and the operating process around the application.

sections.title: My role
body: I owned the application experience, partner commercials, lending operations and P&L. I built the marketplace alongside bank and NBFC onboarding, working with engineering on the lending journey and with growth on distribution through CashKaro’s existing rewards surfaces.

sections.title: What I built
body: The application used common borrower inputs and eligibility-based lender routing. Partner onboarding ran alongside product delivery, covering payout structures, KYC handoffs, service levels and rejection feedback.

Stage-level funnel data, lender MIS and weekly reviews connected observed drop-offs to changes in the application and follow-up process. Reconciliation and dispute tracking made the lender relationship part of the product’s operating system.

sections.title: One application, different lender requirements
body: I designed a common application so an applicant did not have to understand every lender’s policy before starting. Routing used income band, bureau score, employment type and geography to compare the applicant with lender eligibility. The aim was to make lender fit part of the journey before the customer spent time on an unsuitable application.

I ran commercial onboarding in parallel with the reported 30-day build. Each lender conversation covered the payout structure, KYC handoff, service-level expectations and rejection feedback. These details affected the customer journey: a usable form still needed an agreed destination for the case and a way to learn what happened afterwards.

sections.title: A weekly rhythm for improving the funnel
body: I built reporting around lender performance and the stages a case passed through. A daily operations view connected application progress with service levels, payout reconciliation and unresolved disputes. Weekly reviews then followed a practical sequence: pull stage-level drop-offs, form a possible explanation, ship a change and measure what followed.

This also connected product work to commercial accountability. Loan volume, partner payouts and the cost of processing a case sit in the same business, so I owned the P&L alongside the journey. Partner reporting and commercial terms were therefore part of product ownership, and helped bring the customer and business views into the same operating review.

sections.title: What changed
body: The programme reports funnel conversion moving from 16% to 45%, a 29 percentage-point improvement. More than 20 banks and NBFCs formed the broader lending panel. These results describe the marketplace programme, combining routing, partner onboarding, operational follow-through and repeated funnel changes.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: This case connects customer experience with partner policy and operating economics. Its useful product pattern is a shared application with configurable lender differences, supported by measurement that shows where an application loses momentum.

sections.title: The product problem
body: Education lending requires more than presenting a list of lenders. Student and applicant circumstances affect eligibility, documents and the next action. Fragmented lender forms create repeated work for applicants and a difficult case-management process for the people helping them.

sections.title: My role

College.money’s current published discovery surface provides a product reference for this education-loan work. The more detailed policy, document and reviewer journeys are explored in the EduLoans study.

sections.title: Turning student intent into a workable case
body: I mapped the journey from enquiry to application, including the evidence a student needed to collect and the handoffs that could stop a case progressing. The marketplace used a thin origination layer: common application inputs, document collection, eligibility pre-checks and lender routing. This made the case preparation part of the product rather than a separate job left to the applicant.

The marketplace addressed student-lending needs, including upskilling and tier-2/3 applicants. The later EduLoans build gives a more detailed study-abroad matching workflow. College.money is the production education-loan environment identified in the shared portfolio conversation; the marketplace and technical builds are presented as related stages of the work.

sections.title: Building the product and the business together
body: I worked with engineering on the application and lender handoff, with growth on the CashKaro distribution surfaces, and with operations on following the case after submission. MoEngage and internal dashboards made the funnel visible step by step. This let the team discuss the point of abandonment or delay rather than only the final conversion total.

I also owned the commercial partner conversations: pricing, payout structures, KYC responsibilities and service levels. Monetisation was part of the launch design because a completed loan creates both a customer outcome and a partner payout. The integration, student journey and commercial model had to describe the same service before an application could move reliably across the organisations involved.

sections.title: What changed

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: The product contribution is coordinating a complex service into a usable journey. The student application, evidence collection, reviewer work and lender relationship all affect whether an enquiry becomes a workable case. Product and commercial ownership connect those steps with the economics of the service.

caseStudies.title: EduLoans: explainable matching and document operations
caseStudies.summary: A documented rule model, verification gates and two working builds for a complex education-loan workflow.
caseStudies.role: PRD, rule-model and workflow author; AI-assisted prototyping

sections.title: The product problem
body: Different lenders require different eligibility checks and documents. Regional marksheets, scanned tax returns and joint statements also create uncertainty that a pure OCR flow cannot safely resolve. A confident interface can mislead users if the policy underneath it is incomplete.

sections.title: My role
body: I authored the PRD and lender-rule model, chose the initial matching approach and used parallel builds to make the policy and experience reviewable. The portfolio describes a policy/chat prototype alongside a React, TypeScript and Supabase application scaffold.

sections.title: What I built
body: The first version uses deterministic, per-lender eligibility gates and scoring. The model covers 62 rules across eight lender configurations, with scores clamped between 0 and 100 and assigned to five status tiers.

The 23-state workflow requires KAM verification before showing BRE results. Document requirements depend on both lender and applicant type. Classification, validation and verification include a human-review path for uncertain files.

The build deliberately separates policy correctness from application scaffolding. Its documented backlog includes missing lender thresholds, rules-of-record reconciliation and further checklist coverage; these are release work rather than completed outcomes.
bullets: Student, distribution partner and KAM journeys share a common product shell.
Premium-university exceptions, loan amount and income gates remain lender-specific.
The document checklist follows the same policy source as the matching rules.
AI tools are selected for scaffolding, reasoning, review and integration rather than treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: A policy decision that could be inspected
body: I chose deterministic matching for the first release and deferred ML scoring until outcome data existed. I modelled lenders separately: eligibility gates first, then scoring, a 0–100 score boundary and five result tiers. The policy review included premium-university income exceptions, course factors and urgency adjustments. The same inputs and rule version were intended to produce the same answer.

Missing policy was treated as release work. I identified 13 threshold gaps across five lenders and required relationship-manager confirmation with a policy screenshot. The backlog made that a P0 restriction for affected lenders. I also recorded rule-consistency options across the master and two builds: a deploy-time sync with a checksum, or a rules-administration workflow. These were documented controls and launch conditions.

sections.title: Designing for students, partners and reviewers
body: I used one conversational shell to explore three jobs: student capture, partner submission and bulk handling, and KAM queue review. Role-specific conversations and action sheets made those jobs concrete. A separate KAM dashboard later entered the roadmap as the review workload became clearer.

Document requirements came from the lender-by-applicant combination. Classification and extraction could assist a case, while uncertain regional marksheets, tax scans and joint statements had a KAM review path. Verification was a prerequisite for showing a lender match, protecting expectations before the result. The roadmap also included 32 unsecured checklist combinations and operational case views. Emergent, Lovable, Claude, Gemini and Antigravity were used for distinct prototype, scaffold, policy-review and repository tasks.

sections.title: What changed
body: Two working repositories made the policy, prototype and application structure available for review. The broader origination programme reports processing effort falling from nine to four hours per education-loan file, with approximately ₹1,562 in labour value saved per file. Those are workflow-level results rather than separate performance tests of the rules engine, OCR or every prototype screen.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: The design makes uncertainty visible at the point where it affects a decision. Deterministic matching, verification gates and human fallback are documented product choices; production readiness still depends on confirmed lender policies and consistent rules across the builds.

outcomes.label: Eligibility · KYC · status · payouts

sections.title: The product problem
body: A growing lender panel can create repeated engineering work and inconsistent operations. Each partner has its own eligibility, documents, status updates and payout rules. The customer experiences those differences as delays or uncertainty unless the integration and operating process work together.

sections.title: My role
body: I worked on the lender-integration requirements and the partner reporting and review process, alongside engineering, lender teams and operations. The contribution includes the common contract and the business controls around it.

sections.title: What I built
body: The documented contract normalises eligibility, KYC handoff, application status and payouts while preserving lender-specific requirements. Common borrower inputs are carried through configurable partner behaviour.

MIS links lender funnel performance with service levels, payout reconciliation and dispute tracking. Reporting is useful here because an application outcome also creates an operational and commercial follow-through task.

sections.title: Making the common steps explicit
body: I identified the recurring elements of a lender connection: eligibility, KYC handoff, application status and payout information. The API-first design normalised those shared needs so a new partner could fit a common structure while retaining its own policy. I worked directly with engineering on the modular lending stack and the partner reporting around it.

The product and commercial conversations happened together. Payout structure, KYC responsibility and service levels had to be workable for both organisations. Rejection reasons also mattered because an unsuccessful application could reveal a routing issue. This made onboarding a combination of integration requirements, partner commitments and a repeatable operating process.

sections.title: Building an operating team around the integration
body: I recruited across product, sales and operations as the lending business grew from its initial team. Building that cross-functional capability was part of making the marketplace operate after launch. The team’s work connected lender integration with customer applications and day-to-day follow-through.

The daily MIS joined lender-wise funnel performance, partner service-level tracking, disputes and payout reconciliation. An application’s outcome had to be reflected in the business record, and an unresolved dispute needed visibility. The review cadence brought those questions back to lender conversations and product priorities, instead of ending ownership when a request was handed off.

sections.title: What changed
body: The wider lending business reports a panel of more than 20 banks and NBFCs. The integration and MIS work gave the team a common way to follow lender performance, application status, service risks and payout follow-through. It connected the reusable integration structure with the partner and operations work needed to run it.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: This is platform work at the boundary between software and partner operations. The reusable capability is the shared contract; the operating discipline is knowing what happened to each application and whether its outcome was reflected in the business records.

sections.title: The product problem
body: A matching rule embedded in one interface is hard to reuse across products. Lender rejection reasons and reviewer overrides can also reveal gaps in the policy, but the way those signals change future decisions must remain understandable.

sections.title: My role
body: My education-loan MCP work connects lender-rule modelling with a callable policy capability. A later working guide describes personal- and education-loan decision systems behind a shared service; this is a developing architecture account alongside the more concrete EduLoans rules portfolio.

sections.title: What I built
body: The direction is to expose policy evaluation through MCP so a consuming product surface can call the same decision capability. The working guide describes two business-rule engines behind one MCP server, and rejection reasons and manual overrides as feedback inputs. The original technical portfolio retains deterministic matching for the first version.

sections.title: Separating the policy from its interface
body: The working-guide architecture separates a decision capability from the interface consuming it. A chat flow, reviewer surface or another application can have a different interaction pattern while depending on a common lender-policy evaluation. The guide describes two business-rule engines behind one MCP server as the direction for that shared capability.

The initial EduLoans policy work provides the starting point: lender-specific conditions, verification before matching and a source of truth for rules. The service direction extends that work towards reuse. The lender still owns the credit decision, while the product evaluates policy and supports the application handoff.

sections.title: What lender outcomes can tell the product
body: A rejection or underwriter override can point to a missing condition, an unsuitable route or information that was not captured early enough. The later guide describes using those outcomes to review the matching rules. Feedback is a separate part of the design from evaluating the next applicant against the current policy.

That separation matters because changing a policy affects future cases. A deterministic rule can be inspected for one applicant, while an update needs its own ownership and approval process. The workstream brings that operating question into the architecture; production use and the exact update mechanism remain at the development stage described in the source notes.

sections.title: What changed
body: The output is a callable-policy and feedback architecture workstream alongside the working EduLoans builds. It makes the reuse and policy-change questions explicit. There is no separate measured business result for MCP reuse or feedback updates; wider marketplace conversion is covered in its own study.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: This work demonstrates the distinction between an inspectable decision and a policy that can evolve. It also shows why a reusable interface needs an explicit ownership boundary between product rules, reviewer judgement and automated execution.

sections.title: The product problem
body: Commodity trading relied on broker networks, messaging groups and offline contracts. Absolute had a producer-side footprint, but converting that network into transactions required more than publishing a catalogue. Buyers and sellers needed a path through negotiation, payment and trade execution.

sections.title: My role
body: I worked on the mobile and web trading product from its early build, including trader research, process digitisation, requirements and delivery coordination. The March 2022 CV documents investigating payment failures and turning operational issues into product priorities.

sections.title: What I built
body: The marketplace work covers catalogue management, discovery, negotiation and matching. Research with farmers, FPOs and traders helped connect the digital journey to the existing way the business traded.

Payment and ERP workflows formed part of the transaction lifecycle. Regional rollout required coordination across product, engineering, finance, operations and country teams, with customs and trade documentation incorporated into delivery.

sections.title: Working from the way traders already operated
body: I researched farmers, FPOs and rural and small-town traders, including the existing processes and payment failures around live business. The aim was to bring regular trading into a mobile and web marketplace without leaving the difficult operating steps outside the product. sections.title: The product problem
body: UrbanKhet began with terrace farming, while the customer need extended to having fresh produce without doing the growing work. Perishable food creates a tight connection between the order promise, sourcing, harvest timing and delivery.

sections.title: My role
body: I founded UrbanKhet and owned its proposition, web product, customer acquisition, farmer sourcing, team, fulfilment and P&L. I worked directly with early customers and farmers, building the digital order journey and the physical operation as one business.

sections.title: What I built
body: The business pivoted into a farm-to-fork supply chain serving households and businesses. Customer orders were connected to sourcing and delivery through decentralised distribution, operating procedures and a web product.

The records report a 28-person team and a farmer network built through outreach and local relationships. Enterprise customers included Marriott, BigBasket, Udaan and Ninjacart alongside the consumer business.

sections.title: From terrace farming to a paid customer promise
body: UrbanKhet began with terrace farming. The later proposition served consumers who wanted fresh produce without taking on the work of growing it. I acquired the first 44 customers manually and developed farmer supply through cold outreach and local relationships. Those activities built the initial demand and supply sides before the venture had an established customer base.

I pivoted towards direct farm-to-consumer distribution, then developed household subscription plans and business demand around the same sourcing operation. Serving a household and serving a hotel or marketplace created different buyer relationships, while both depended on produce arriving in usable condition. I owned business development and the fulfilment behind those commitments.

sections.title: A web product supported by distributed operations
body: I developed the web product and operating workflows, with decentralised urban distribution in Maharashtra and Gujarat described in the Professional Profile. Sourcing, inventory, harvest timing and last-mile delivery had to work together. SOPs gave the team repeatable routines rather than making the customer promise depend only on individual improvisation.

The March 2022 CV reports a maximum of 10% wastage, compared with a stated 35% industry benchmark. That is a level achieved in the described operation, not a company before-and-after reduction. The later profile describes a six-hour harvest-to-home model. Both belong to the physical service design, where quality, timing and cost affected the venture’s economics.

sections.title: What changed
body: The venture reports a 28-person team, more than 3,600 clients and 45 business customers. Marriott, BigBasket, Udaan and Ninjacart are among the named accounts. The farmer network is reported at more than 3,000. These are distinct views of the business: the team delivering it, the demand it served and the suppliers it connected.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: The founder contribution is the connection between a digital product and its physical promise. Customer learning, supplier trust, team routines and unit economics all shape whether an order can be fulfilled reliably.

sections.title: The product problem

sections.title: My role

sections.title: What I built
body: The reported pivot rebuilt the logistics chain within 15 days and included decentralised delivery collaboration with Amul. Sourcing, customer demand and route planning had to be reconsidered as one system.

sections.title: Changing the model as demand and access changed
body: I assessed the disruption to business-customer demand and the practical constraints on moving produce. The pivot put greater emphasis on direct consumer demand while revising distribution. Logistics partnerships and route planning were treated as part of the same change because a new order channel still needed a route that could fulfil the order.

The Professional Profile describes rebuilding that logistics chain within fifteen days and creating decentralised delivery collaboration with Amul. Delivery routes changed with daily volume. My responsibility as founder covered those decisions and the operating team together; a route adjustment or partnership was useful only if the service could continue under the new constraints.

sections.title: Leadership through a changing operating reality
body: The 28-person team remained part of my founder remit while the venture changed its customer and delivery model. I continued operating the business, coordinating the team and revising the service under lockdown conditions. The people, customer commitments and economics were connected parts of that responsibility.

The later account records a decision to wind down after the second wave made the economics unsustainable. Ownership extended to assessing whether continued operation remained viable, as well as making the first-wave pivot. body: I captained FC Sparta at CEPT University and maintain an independent painting practice, mainly in oils. Both sit outside my employment record and provide personal context alongside the product portfolio.

sections.title: What I built
body: The football account describes taking over a team that had finished near the bottom and subsequently winning three consecutive championships. Captaincy is the contribution retained here, without adding an undocumented training or selection method.

Painting remains an active independent visual practice. Actual work and images can show its character more clearly than a commercial design claim; the practice is included as a personal part of the portfolio.

sections.title: What changed
body: Three consecutive championships are reported in the supplied profile. No quantified result is attached to the painting practice, and neither activity is used as a substitute for evidence of professional team management.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: This supporting case shows interests and leadership outside formal product roles. Its contribution to the portfolio is personal context supported by actual work and records, rather than an invented causal link to later business performance.

sections.title: The product problem
body: The supplied exercise asks how a paid membership can provide recurring value after an immediate liquidity need has passed. Earlier material frames this as a fragmented ecosystem and proposes a Credit Cockpit; later material explores credit utility and merchant-funded benefits.

sections.title: My role
body: I authored strategy presentations and a cohort-retention diagnostic. This is an independent portfolio exercise, not MoneyLion employment, a commissioned client engagement or evidence of a launched MoneyLion product.

sections.title: What I built
body: The Credit Cockpit version proposes linking financial-product surfaces, secured-credit utility and proactive credit-management features. These are proposals whose technical, partner and regulatory feasibility would need validation.

The later 60-slide work develops merchant-funded cashback, cash-flow-based lender matching, a visible membership ROI dashboard and a staged pilot. It distinguishes settled rewards from estimates, keeps merchant spend separate from membership acquisition cost and describes outcome and contribution guardrails.

The retention diagnostic focuses on repeated use rather than launch sign-ups. Bounty Utilization Rate is defined as the share of a paid-start cohort completing at least two qualifying transactions within 90 days. The sample curves and financial scenarios illustrate the method; they are not observed MoneyLion results.
bullets: Evaluate repeated member value rather than sign-up volume alone.
Keep estimated benefit separate from realised, settled member value.
Connect customer outcomes, credit quality and contribution before scaling.
Treat partner and regulatory feasibility as validation work, rather than a completed launch claim.

sections.title: A cohort contract for recurring value
body: The later proposal defines BUR90 around every first-time paid WOW start whose cohort has reached day 90. The numerator is members completing at least two distinct qualifying D2C Mega-Cashback transactions, with purchase and settlement by day 90. Cancelled, refunded and inactive starts remain in the denominator; referrals, reversals and split-order duplicates do not count as qualifying transactions.

The proposed measurement records offer version, settlement time and reversal status. D7 profile activation, a D30 first settled reward and D60 second-order progression serve as leading signals, while pending rewards stay separate. This makes the repeat-use question more precise than a launch-sign-up count or a chart of active members alone.

sections.title: A proposed pilot, with explicit assumptions
body: The latest 60-slide deck proposes two main bets: merchant-funded CPA cashback passed through to members, and cash-flow-first lender-approved matching. Fee-free Instacash utility and a membership ROI dashboard support those bets. The execution proposal starts with consent, data quality, quote contracts and funded merchant supply before scaling referrals, personalisation and lifecycle prompts.

Every number here is a planning assumption from the exercise. The initial pilot proposes ten merchant partners, 25 by month three and 50 by month four. Proposed gates include a D30 first-bounty rate of at least 40%, at least 99% correct settlement, and BUR90 of at least 60% with a ten percentage-point lift over generic ranking. A six-month plan assumes twelve core roles plus shared Risk/Finance support and an illustrative $980,000 budget. None is an achieved MoneyLion result.

sections.title: Scale, repair or stop based on the mechanism
body: The proposal assigns failure responses to the underlying constraint: repair data coverage or lender fit, fix reward tracking and merchant supply, simplify ranking if a holdout shows no incremental value, or stop acquisition when economics fail. Earned rewards remain protected. Permissioned messaging and referral caps are proposed safeguards rather than evidence of a launched policy.

The earlier Credit Cockpit decks explore a different route through credit utilisation, secured-credit utility and a data/dispute centre. The retention diagnostic and later deck are separate iterations of the exercise. The deliverable is a set of inspectable bets, flows, economic assumptions and experiments, with partner, risk and commercial validation still required.

sections.title: What changed
body: The outputs are strategy documents, product-flow concepts, a proposed experimentation plan and an economic model. No delivered conversion, credit-score, retention or contribution-margin improvement is claimed. Older and later deck versions contain different bets and assumptions, which remain versions of the exercise rather than one implemented programme.

sections.title: The lesson from this work
body: This case demonstrates product reasoning that connects user value, business economics and a testable measurement contract. The strength of the exercise is making the proposed mechanism and validation plan inspectable, while keeping an illustrative model separate from a business result.
